newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa rand at 7-week high, mood upbeat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa rand at 7-week high, mood upbeat.

text.p: The South African rand on Friday rallied to its best level against the U.S. dollar since early December as foreign demand fed a growing mood of optimism.

Dealers said a consensus was emerging that the rand would stabilise in 1997, falling a modest 6-7 percent in line with inflation differentials, after its 29 percent slide against the greenback in 1996.

"I think we are in for a different ball game this year on the rand," said Peter Lane, head of treasury at UAL Merchant Bank. "The rand is going to trade in a much tighter band this year. It will depreciate, but at a controlled rate broadly in line with inflation differentials."
The currency was briefly quoted at 4.6300/6350 against the dollar on Friday -- its firmest level in seven weeks -- before easing slightly to around 4.64 in the afternoon.

Economists argue that while economic growth will be weak in 1997, the balance of payments position will improve sharply. That in turn will boost low foreign reserves which have made the rand a target for speculators.
Hania Farhan of ING Barings expects South Africa to record a trade surplus of $3.1 billion in 1997, up from $2.2 billion in 1996.

"The positive impact of the depreciation on the export sector will only come through fully in 1997. At the same time, imports will be increasingly constrained following a fair amount of pre-emptive buying in 1996," she said.
Foreign reserves stood at just $2.2 billion in December, equivalent to less than four weeks' import cover, but some analysts believe they could be back at $4.0 billion by end-1997.

The market mood is also being helped by signs of fiscal rectitude on the part of the government, with latest figures showing government revenue up a healthy 17 percent in the first nine months of the year.
"The latest figures show revenues are doing very well, although income tax is enjoying a boost from economic growth which is now in the past," said Dawie Roodt, economist at brokerage Equisec.

Government bonds also firmed markedly on Friday as a steadier rand encouraged buyers, particularly from overseas. Long bond yields have now fallen some 60 basis points to the best levels in three months.

One fly in the ointment is the daily money market shortage, which remains stubbornly above 10 billion rand. But traders said the market was largely unperturbed by the squeeze at the short-end, predicting short-term rates would ease if the rand steadied in the medium term, boosting inflows into the country.
That could pave the way for a bank rate cut around mid-year. Bank rate currently stands at 17 percent with prime at 20.25 percent.
